label: Qualitative Picture
notes: This closing chapter of Part I, printed pages 333 through 352, gathers a hundred theorems into one coherent picture. For the quadratic cost the optimal plan is a deterministic map, that map is the gradient of a convex potential, and the same transport admits a static, a dynamic, and a Lagrangian reading that all agree.

label: Static Kantorovich Picture
notes: Start from the Kantorovich relaxation: minimise the average cost over couplings with fixed marginals. The minimum always exists by compactness, the optimum concentrates on a c-cyclically monotone set, and Kantorovich duality pairs it with a potential whose c-transform certifies optimality. This is the robust backbone everything else refines.

label: Brenier's Map
notes: Under the squared distance and an absolutely continuous source, the optimal plan collapses to a single-valued map equal to the gradient of a convex function. Brenier's theorem fuses optimal transport with convex analysis: no mass is split, and the convex potential is unique up to an additive constant.

label: Cyclical Monotonicity
notes: Cyclical monotonicity is the geometric fingerprint of optimality: no finite cycle of source-target pairs can be rearranged to lower the total cost. For the quadratic cost this is exactly the subdifferential of a convex function, which is why the map turns out to be a gradient. The support never crosses itself wastefully.

label: Monge-Ampere Equation
notes: Pushing the source density through the map and conserving mass yields a Jacobian equation. With the map a convex gradient, its Jacobian is the Hessian of the potential, so mass conservation becomes the Monge-Ampere equation. This fully nonlinear PDE is the analytic face of the map and the gateway to regularity theory.

label: Displacement Interpolation
notes: Interpolate by letting each particle travel along the straight segment from its source to its Brenier image at constant speed. The resulting path of measures is a constant-speed geodesic of the Wasserstein space, and McCann's displacement interpolation is the curve along which energies become convex. Interpolation can expose regularity the endpoints hide.

label: Benamou-Brenier Dynamics
notes: The dynamic viewpoint replaces the static plan with a fluid flow. A density and a velocity field obey the continuity equation, and minimising the integrated kinetic energy recovers the squared Wasserstein distance. Benamou and Brenier turned transport into a least-action fluid-mechanics problem, with the optimal velocity a gradient field along the geodesic.

label: Lagrangian Least Action
notes: The Lagrangian reading follows individual trajectories rather than the whole density. Each particle minimises an action, the trajectories are geodesics in the base space, and they never cross before the final time. This least-action picture connects optimal transport to classical mechanics and Hamilton-Jacobi theory through the evolving potential.

label: Three Equivalent Viewpoints
notes: The chapter's central dictionary: static Kantorovich plans, dynamic Benamou-Brenier flows, and Lagrangian action-minimising trajectories are three descriptions of one object. The convex potential generates the map, the map generates the geodesic, and the geodesic's velocity solves the continuity equation. Translating between columns is the working skill of the theory.

label: Regularity Picture
notes: Regularity asks whether a smooth source and target force a smooth map. The answer depends on the geometry of the target support: convexity of the target domain is essentially necessary, and counterexamples show the map can be discontinuous otherwise. Caffarelli's theory and the Ma-Trudinger-Wang condition organise when the Monge-Ampere solution stays smooth.

label: The Decision Map
notes: The notebook recasts Part I as a decision flow: each assumption unlocks a conclusion. Absolute continuity buys a map, the quadratic cost buys a convex potential, target convexity buys regularity. The coded invariant checks that every conclusion node is reachable from some assumption path, making the chapter's hidden hypotheses visible and testable.

label: Launchpad to Part II
notes: This consolidated picture is the springboard for Part II. Displacement interpolation and the geodesic structure of Wasserstein space let us read Ricci curvature lower bounds as convexity of entropy along geodesics. The static, dynamic, and Lagrangian dictionary built here becomes the language of curvature, gradient flows, and synthetic geometry.
